newsitem.title: GERMANY: "New oldies" to boost German tourist trade.
newsitem.headline: "New oldies" to boost German tourist trade.

text.p: Germany's tourist trade expects an emerging group of "new oldies", or affluent travellers over 50, to drive industry growth of two to four percent this year, executives told a tourism fair which began on Tuesday.
Gerd Hesselmann, president of the German Travel Bureau Association, told the fair that the rising population of older travellers would become an increasingly interesting target for travel agents.
"These people will in future be better educated, healthier, wealthier, more mobile and consumer-oriented than the same age group 10 or 20 years ago," Hesselmann said.
He added that the winter season was going well, with hotels booked out at Christmas. But, after a good season last year, double-digit growth could not be expected.
Commenting on market trends, Hesselmann said the German tourism market was becoming more polarised, with the premium and budget segments expanding strongly while the mid-price sector weakens.
Germans spent 156 billion marks ($91.4 billion) on overnight travel in 1995 -- 95 billion marks of it abroad -- making them the world's most avid international travellers, the association said.
About 4.2 percent of German private consumption is spent on travel. Germany's tourist industry, which employs two million people, had sales totalling 43 billion marks in 1995/96.

Spain was the most popular destination for German tourists, luring 12.6 percent, followed by Italy, Austria, France and Greece. Long-distance travel, including the United States and Canada, attracted 11.4 percent.
Market research also shows that Germans are increasingly choosing to travel to foreign destinations, and holidays abroad could reach 75 to 80 percent of the total by the year 2000.
Germany's biggest five travel agents are TUI, with turnover of 5.3 billion marks; NUR with 3.4 billion; LTT with 2.9 billion; DER with 1.4 billion and ITS with 925 million marks.

Three-fifths of holidays are individual trips, while the remaining 40 percent are group tours. Some 52 percent of holidaymakers travelled by car, 28 percent by aeroplane, 9.8 percent by bus and eight percent by rail.

Germany's domestic tourism industry recorded over 300 million overnight stays last year, of which 10 percent were by foreign travellers. Strongest growth came in the states of former east Germany, said Juergen Werner, chief executive of the German Tourism Association. ($ = 1.707 German Marks)
